skill.name: refactoring
skill.description: Guides safe code refactoring through one structural change, one test run, and one commit at a time. It focuses on cleanup, extraction, renaming, and simplification without changing behavior.
skill.summary: Guides behavior-preserving refactors through small tested steps.
skill.author: ArcadeAI

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown fences and inline code examples, not executable backtick shell usage. No evidence of prompt injection, network access, credential access, or data exfiltration was found. Two semantic risks remain: wildcard tool permissions and revert guidance that could discard uncommitted work without confirmation.

remediation.suggestion: Replace allowed-tools: '*' with the narrow tools required for reading files, editing files, running tests, and safe git operations.
Require explicit user confirmation and show affected files before running git checkout, git restore, or any command that discards changes.

remediation.issue: Markdown command examples trigger noisy static findings
remediation.suggestion: Use prose for shell guidance when possible, or label examples as manual commands that require user approval.

static_findings.snippet: | Long function        | **Extract Function** | Pull 10 lines into `calculateTax()`    |
| Unnecessary variable | **Inline Variable**  | Remove `temp = x; return temp;`        |
| Misplaced code       | **Move Function**    | Move `validate()` to `Validator` class |
| Complex conditional | **Decompose Conditional** | Extract `if` branches to named functions
- Did it accidentally change behavior? → Reconsider approach

semantic_findings.title: Unrestricted Tool Permission
semantic_findings.description: The frontmatter declares allowed-tools: '*', which grants broad tool access if the host honors it. A refactoring skill should use a narrower permission set because it works with local files, tests, and git.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The wildcard permission is explicit on line 4 and applies to the whole skill. The risk is permission breadth, not evidence of malicious behavior.

semantic_findings.title: Destructive Revert Command Encouraged
semantic_findings.description: The workflow says to revert immediately when tests fail and shows git checkout -- <changed-files>. This can discard uncommitted user work if run without confirming ownership of the changed files.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The revert instruction and command are directly present in the file. The impact depends on agent behavior and user confirmation, so the severity is medium.

content.user_title: Refactor Code in Small Verified Steps
content.value_statement: Large refactors can change behavior and hide regressions. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through small tested changes with commits after each safe step.
actual_capabilities: Identifies refactoring requests and separates them from bug fixes or new features.
Requires characterization tests before changing code with weak coverage.
Applies one refactoring at a time, such as rename, extract function, or guard clauses.
Runs tests after each structural change and stops when behavior changes.
Uses commits to isolate successful refactoring steps.
Provides rollback guidance after failed refactor attempts.
limitations: Does not add product features or intentional behavior changes.
Depends on runnable tests or time to add characterization tests.
May require user judgment for brittle tests, hidden dependencies, or large design changes.
Includes broad tool permissions and revert guidance that should be reviewed before installation.

use_cases.title: Clean Up Legacy Functions
use_cases.description: Improve unclear names, long functions, and nested conditionals while preserving current behavior.

use_cases.title: Prepare Code Before Feature Work
use_cases.description: Reduce technical debt before adding new behavior, using tests to protect existing outcomes.

use_cases.title: Teach Safe Refactoring Discipline
use_cases.description: Guide engineers through small changes, test checks, and clear commits after each successful step.

prompt_templates.title: Clean Up One Function
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner request for a narrow refactor.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the refactoring skill on this function. First assess whether it is refactoring, then make one safe change and run tests.

prompt_templates.title: Add Safety Tests First
prompt_templates.scenario: Moderate request for code with limited coverage.
prompt_templates.prompt: This module has limited tests. Add characterization tests for the behavior you will touch, then complete the smallest useful refactor.

prompt_templates.title: Refactor a Class Incrementally
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate request for a larger unit of code.
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor this class without changing behavior. Break the work into separate rename, extract, or move steps, testing after each step.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Large Restructure
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced request that may span several safe steps.
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze this large refactoring request. Propose the smallest safe sequence, identify test gaps, and stop before any behavior-changing work.

output: Classifies the request as refactoring, not feature work.
Checks or adds tests for current discount behavior.
Renames unclear values and runs tests before committing.

output_examples.input: Clean up this class with too many responsibilities.
output: Moves one method or group at a time.
Stops after each passing test run for review.
Explains that behavior may have changed.
Asks how to proceed before further edits.

best_practices: Keep each refactoring small enough to explain in one sentence.
Add characterization tests before changing code with weak coverage.
Review commits after each passing test run.
anti_patterns: Combining renames, extracts, and behavior changes in one edit.
Treating failed tests as bugs to fix inside the refactor.
Running destructive revert commands without confirming affected files.

faq.question: What is this skill for?
faq.answer: It guides behavior-preserving code cleanup through small tested refactoring steps.

faq.question: Can it add new features?
faq.answer: No. It should redirect feature work and bug fixes to a different workflow.

faq.question: Does it require tests?
faq.answer: Yes. It asks for existing tests or characterization tests before risky structural changes.

faq.question: What refactorings does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers renaming, extracting functions, inlining variables, guard clauses, moving code, and removing dead code.

faq.question: How does it handle failures?
faq.answer: It stops after failed tests and asks the user to decide the next step after repeated failures.

faq.question: Is it safe to install automatically?
faq.answer: Review it first because it declares broad tool access and includes revert command guidance.
